lesson.title: Why Did They Do That? The Hidden Rules of Everyday Mind-Reading
lesson.summary: Attribution theory studies how people explain the causes of behavior, distinguishing internal from external explanations, and identifies systematic biases like the fundamental attribution error that shape those everyday judgments.
lesson.body:
Psychology as a science is built on studying behavior and mental processes systematically rather than relying on gut assumptions. Attribution theory turns that same systematic lens on something everyone does constantly and informally: explaining why people, including ourselves, behave the way they do. Fritz Heider, often credited as the theory's originator, described ordinary people as something like naive psychologists, constantly generating causal explanations for behavior as a basic part of making sense of the social world.

Those explanations, called attributions, generally sort into two broad types. A dispositional, or internal, attribution explains behavior by pointing to something about the person: their personality, ability, character, or mood. A situational, or external, attribution explains behavior by pointing to something about the circumstances, context, or environment the person is in. The same behavior, like showing up late, can be explained either way: as evidence that someone is inconsiderate, or as the result of unusually heavy traffic that morning.

This is also where the schemas you learned about become directly relevant: attributions are rarely built from scratch through careful reasoning, they're generated quickly using existing schemas and expectations about people and situations, which is efficient but also a source of systematic error. The best documented of these errors is the fundamental attribution error, the tendency, identified by researcher Lee Ross, to overestimate dispositional causes and underestimate situational causes when explaining other people's behavior. Someone who cuts you off in traffic gets labeled reckless far more readily than probably rushing to an emergency, even though both are possible.

Related biases round out the picture. The actor-observer difference describes how we tend to explain our own behavior more situationally, blaming traffic for our own lateness, while explaining the identical behavior in someone else more dispositionally, assuming they're just always late. Self-serving bias describes the tendency to attribute our own successes to disposition and our own failures to situational factors, a pattern that helps protect self-esteem and self-efficacy after setbacks. Building on this, psychologist Bernard Weiner extended attribution theory by describing attributions along dimensions like locus, internal versus external, stability, stable versus changeable over time, and controllability, and linked particular combinations to specific emotions and motivation: pride after an internal, controllable success, shame after an internal, uncontrollable failure, and so on.

This attributional lens is also exactly what researchers used to sharpen the learned helplessness model covered earlier in this unit: someone who explains a failure as internal, stable, and global, believing they always mess everything up, is left far more vulnerable to sliding into pervasive helplessness than someone who explains the identical failure as external, unstable, and specific, chalking it up to one badly written test. The pattern of attributions a person habitually makes turns out to shape not just how they understand a single event, but how resilient or helpless they become in the face of future setbacks.
